 O Lord Jesus Christ, most merciful Father, I beseech You with my whole heart that You may forgive all my sins in this present life, that You may punish me for them, and that You may not reserve any punishment for purgatory. ### ¶ Monday
### ¶ Nocturn

**L**ady, may the splendor of your countenance be my illumination, and may the serenity of your grace shine upon my mind. Lift up my head above my enemies, and I shall sing; I shall sing a psalm to your name. Turn not your face away from me, for I have desired your beauty and your grace from my youth. I have loved you, O Queen of Heaven, and I have sought your mercy; do not withdraw your grace from your servant. I will confess you among the nations, and I will honor the throne of your glory. Glory.

**U**nto you, O Lady, I will cry out, and you shall hear me; in the voice of your praise, you shall gladden me. Have mercy on me in the day of my distress, and in the light of your truth, deliver me. Blessed be you, O Lady, in all the ends of the world. The sanctuary which your hands have established is the holy temple of your body. Your conscience is pure and immaculate, the place

———— page break ————

of propitiation and the dwelling place of the holy of holies. 
Bring to our Lady, sons of God: bring to our Lady, our praise and reverence. 
Grant strength to your servants, holy Mother: and blessing to those who praise and glorify you. Hear the sighs of those who sigh unto you: and do not despise the vows of those who call upon your name. May your hand be prepared to help me: and may your ear be attentive to my prayer. May the heavens and the earth, the sea and the circuit of the earth, bless you. 
I will exalt you, O Lady, because you have taken me up: you shall deliver me from the unjust adversary. Turn to me and give me life: bring me back from the gates of death: and from the waves of tribulations which have surrounded me. 
Because of your power and the magnificence of your right hand, crush and scatter all my adversaries. And I shall offer to you a sacrifice of praise: and I shall more devoutly exalt your glory. Exult, O heavens, and rejoice, O earth: for Mary will comfort her children: and she will have mercy on her poor. 
In you, O Lady, have I hoped, I shall not be confounded forever: in your grace, take me up.

On the public utility of our citizens, and by what method that matter might be better managed by us, I have decided to write to you, so that I might open the reasoning of all my deliberations to you first. I have often perceived in my mind how the revenues and other proceeds of our city might be greatly increased without any inconvenience to our citizens or our allies. To accomplish this matter, I saw that I had need of your counsel and prudence. You are not unaware that for many years past, neither merchants nor the publicans (being moved by the fear of pirates) were able to navigate this sea of ours safely, from which it happens that our revenues have come in at a much lower amount. …. Farewell.

 I know that you are eager for new things, and that you have often accused me because I never write to you about these matters. I do so today, so that henceforth you cannot blame my negligence. I fill you not with common rumors (as many are accustomed to do), nor with false ones, but with great reports for which I have credible authors. Certain men sailed here to our city from Egypt , from whom our citizens, having inquired diligently about all matters, reported that a few days after the ship had departed, many nations of the East and most of the southern peoples had fled. They said that the King himself, suspecting nothing of the kind, had rushed out from the royal city to meet the enemies, and with his entire army, had been caught in the ambush of the foes. Not long after, enemy standards were moved toward the city of Alexandria , and in the panic, flight was ordered in every direction. Some headed for the Red Sea , others indeed for Libya . Many also went there, driven by fear. As to what happened next, they say they have nothing certain, except that with winds blowing at their sterns, they maintained a prosperous course to us with great speed. If this is true, much

I do not doubt, from what is written to me, that our men who are in Egypt will suffer the greatest losses, as they have placed their own money in the beginning of new things in another region. For there are high matters that lead me into the greatest fear, for if that barbarian nation should reach the city of Alexandria , the same ruin will often drag down not only the wealth of the Egyptians, but also that of all who remain there trading from many parts. If, however, it must remain long under siege, it is to be feared that the money of the merchants will be exhausted by the costs of war, and they will use both public and private money. For since I had placed all my money in that place in previous years, I fear that in one day all my fortunes will be destroyed, unless my agents make good use of advice in time. I desire to be made more certain by you regarding all things. If anyone by chance should sail to us from the East, you will take care that whatever fortune our affairs have undergone, there is nothing that remains hidden from you by me. Farewell.

*Appeal to a General Council.*

The thunders of the Vatican were now being prepared; Noailles was judged by the College of Cardinals itself to be unworthy of the purple. Nevertheless, time was still given to repent, from the hope that the Opponents had shown by having completed a certain scheme of doctrine, which, when it was not approved by those accepting, they offered them a writing of three columns, similar to that Jansenist one of old, in the middle column of which were the propositions of Quesnell themselves, on one side the obvious sense, on the other some other Catholic one, or at least one capable of excuse

it was read with patience. But neither could this satisfy, and glosses were added by those accepting the bull , by which they demonstrated that the obvious sense of the propositions had been rightly condemned, and that they could possess no other meaning unless through a violent distortion. Yet, lest every hope perish once more along with this matter, Cardinal Rohan persuaded the Bishop of Orléans to convene an assembly of Bishops on November 20, 1716, in which the Acceptantes might propose some explanation of the Bull. Christ in the Holy Supper offered the same thing to all to be eaten and drunk, that is, the same to Judas Iscariot and to John the Evangelist. Therefore, Judas Iscariot received the same thing as John the Evangelist, albeit with different fruit: Judas, indeed, to his destruction, but John, to his salvation. Sie primam damnabant propositionem, dicebantque, justis omnibus dari gratiam, qua ipsis mandata Dei possibilia fiant, si eam a Deo, ut oportet, petant: sed animo retinebant, gratiam orandi, ut oportet, non omnibus justis dari. Secundam damnabant, quia gratiæ parvæ Jansenii, quæ desiderium boni debile tantum in nobis excitat, inferior simul est delectatione terrestri, (intellige) cui vincendæ sufficiens non est, utique resisti potest: quia, apud se addunt, semper resistitur. In tertia damnarunt, & rejecerunt ex animo necessitatem (puta) naturalem, seu physicam, quæ non per electionem, sed per impulsum facit agere. All good men were stunned, until Saint-André, the Vicar of Bossuet, who as a witness and arbiter knew all that had been done by the Bishop in this matter, exposed the most disgraceful frauds. Then indeed the indignation of all erupted, the work was reported to the sacred tribunals, and antidotes against the plague were sought. Meanwhile, Quesnel, having been established as the head of the faction after Arnauld, and Gerberon, by scattering seditious pamphlets through Belgium and Gaul, as was related above, and having taken opportunity especially from the aforementioned casus conscientiæ , threw everything into confusion; and by now the unbridled license of these men seemed to be curable only by the application of force. But this was a difficult labor. Quesnel, by frequently changing his hideouts and clothes, and using fictitious names—at times called Father Prior, or Provincial of the Augustinians, at other times Monsieur de Fresne, Frekerberg, Baron de Rebeck, du Puis, etc.—had up to that point eluded the industry of the most sagacious men.

…blasphemy, or disparagement or cursing. For it must be believed that this spirit conducts itself after the manner of a beggar, who laments his defects, begging for aid and alms from the living. And this is a sign of good hope, and one should believe it is permitted to him by a special grace from God, because perhaps he has no other consolation except the common suffrages of the church, to whom God has mercifully granted that he may also beg for special ones. For the virtue of humility, in whoever it may appear, cannot be without grace, the scripture saying: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." For from the proud, as from mountains, water is wont to flow down to the valleys of humility. And on the mountains of Gilboa, neither dew nor rain is wont to pour itself, 2 Samuel 1.

Other signs of the discernment of spirits could be found, but these five may suffice for now. But I wish to be prompt to the pious reader that I do not define those things that were said before concerning ceremonies, persons, priests, places, times, or signs, prayers, masses, fasts, etc., as always being so necessary that revelation or knowledge of spirits can never occur without them, because

———— page break ————

and sometimes it can happen without them. For it is clear that the souls of the deceased reveal themselves to the living or vice versa, a father to his son or vice versa, a mother to her daughter and vice versa, a brother to his brother, etc., without those aforementioned things. But where no other certainty can be had, and a spirit's apparition is perceived, then such a method is probably believed to be observed. It is necessary, therefore, in this shadowy matter to proceed under a certain type and exemplification, just as Aristotle teaches in the first book of the Ethics , because demonstrations are not sought here, but it is necessary to know the truth from probabilities and signs as much as one can. Nor is it impossible that that spirit also sometimes molests some people by pulling hair, dragging away clothes, slapping, etc., for this purpose: so that it may imprint credibility upon itself and make the person attentive, so that he does not disregard it and pass over the vision lightly. As we read in the fourth book of Gregory’s Dialogues concerning the Bishop of Narni, whose chaplain saw a vision and delayed in informing him; therefore, he was severely beaten for the third time…

All good men were stunned, until Saint-André, Bossuet's Vicar, who as a witness and arbiter knew everything that had been done by the Bishop in this matter, exposed the most disgraceful frauds. Then indeed the indignation of all erupted, the work was referred to the sacred tribunals, and antidotes against the plague were sought. Meanwhile, Quesnel, having been established as the head of the faction after Arnauld, and Gerberon, having scattered seditious pamphlets throughout Belgium and Gaul as was reported above, taking occasion especially from the aforementioned case of conscience, threw everything into confusion; and by now the unbridled license of those men seemed to be restrainable only by the application of force. But this was the difficult task. Quesnel, by frequently changing his hideouts, his clothing, and his assumed names—now called Father Prior or Provincial of the Augustinians, now Monsieur de Fresne, Frekerberg, Baron de Rebeck, du Puis, etc.—had hitherto eluded the diligence of the most sagacious men.

Non hic viri hujus vitæ historiam texere lubet, duo tantum iis, quæ jam de eo dicta sunt, memoratu digna juvat addere. Primum est scriptum quoddam ab ipso Quesnello Sacerdoti cuidam missum, qui abstersa tandem errorum caligine, sibi, & Ecclesiæ redditus illud prodidit. Regulæ erant 12. articulis comprehensæ, quibus sui in conversatione inter se & cum vario hominum genere uterentur. Summa ferme hæc erat: Unio, & concordia: arcani fides: circumspectio in sermone pro varia hominum conditione: amphibologia in variis capitibus Religionis: uti Christum in Eucharistia præsentem, neque tantum per fidem, aut figuram, ut heterodoxi, sed neque per transubstantiationem, aut substantialiter, sive realiter, ut Catholici ajunt, dici volebat: quomodo igitur? modo imperceptibili. These were rules comprised in 12 articles, which his own were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. For the virtue of humility, in whoever it may appear, cannot be without grace, the scripture saying: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." And on the mountains of Gilboa, neither dew nor rain is accustomed to pour itself out, 2 Kings 1.

Other signs of the discernment of spirits could be found, but these five suffice for now. Some clergy agree with the godless mobs; they bear the name of clergy, but in truth, they are spiritless, and by their fruits, one can recognize whose children they are, for every tree is known by its fruits. You despise God’s servants and slander them. Just as the Pharisees said to the Lord Christ when He set the truth before their eyes and exposed their gross vices: Master, with these words you insult us. That is how it goes in our Christianity today. Who is it then that insults the pious preachers? Live like a Christian, teach simply, draw your listeners to true Christianity, to a godly life and constant repentance, and lead

an exemplary life yourself, go before your listeners with good examples, then you have a good conscience, and these speeches concern you not at all. Thereby they certainly give it to be understood that they are true Pharisees, since they make use of what the Lord Christ said of them: Namely,
> What they tell you, do; but you should not act according to their works.

Such godless clergymen will, however, also have to hear on the Last Day what the Lord Christ says there:

For there must be, as much for teacher as for listener, a fruitful branch on the vine of Christ, and the preachers must also lead a truly Christian life in Christ, so that they do not, as the Holy Apostle Paul says:
> Preach to others and become reprobate themselves.

…, since the Son of God works everywhere, it must be that his flesh is present everywhere.* Answer. In this place, Osiander rehashes and casts back at us the first argument of the Apollinarian heretics, who attributed Deity to the flesh of Christ, just as a soul is attributed to a body. Furthermore, the very likeness used by Osiander overturns the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ. For just as a soul, even though hypostatically united to a body, does not exercise all its operations through the body, such as meditating, reasoning, and the like: so too the Deity of Christ does not perfect all its actions through his humanity, even after the union. Therefore, it does not conclude that it is present everywhere.

 Page 28. *The humanity assumed by Christ is one person with his own Deity, and is hypostatically united with it. Therefore, wherever the Deity of Christ is, there also is his flesh or humanity.* Answer. First, this man formerly took the presence of Christ in the Lord’s Supper not from the hypostatic union, but from these words of Christ: "This is my body." Next, recognizing that this protection of his is weak, he now abandons it, and turns himself toward the hypostatic union.

Noailles was terrified all the more by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in upholding its acts. In the year 1727, many bishops had gathered at Embrun to overthrow the monstrous errors which were being scattered here and there by the schismatics, and to compose the disturbances incited by the same. There were, furthermore, two principal acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer of the monastery of Sainte-Geneviève, along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist—who, intending to carry out the system of Dupin , crossed over into England and exalted himself there with other writings on the ordinations of Anglican bishops—and the other, the sentence passed on September 20th against Soanen, Bishop of Senez. A certain pastoral instruction had appeared under his name, teeming with infamous errors of every kind, and in which, to the extent that the work of Quesnel was commended, the Bull condemning it was held up as worthy of every execration. This instruction was condemned

———— page break ————

by the bishops; he himself was summoned to the council to give an account. Soanen, having initially prevaricated, and thirteen bishops having been named before whom he might plead his case, and against whom he himself had no objections to raise, finally set out for Embrun, not without a profane retinue, which was not unarmed. But before he entered the city, he had it announced to the assembled bishops that he would never recognize them as judges. Subsequently, when asked by the Council if that Instruction was his, he indeed denied that it had been composed by him, nevertheless professing openly that he entirely adopted, held, and approved it as his own until he could be convinced of the errors which the bishops had condemned in it. In truth, the obstinacy of this man could not be overcome. Therefore, by the sentence of the Council, he was interdicted from every function, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese. It would be tedious to recount the outcries and tumults this scene produced. Twelve bishops protested against this sentence and brought a formal protest to the King himself. Noailles was terrified all the more by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in upholding its acts. Many bishops had gathered at Embrun in the year 1727 to overthrow the immense errors that were being scattered everywhere by the schismatics and to settle the disturbances stirred up by them. Furthermore, there were two principal acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer from the monastery of Saint Genevieve along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, who, intending to execute the system of Dupin , crossed over into England, and raised himself there with other writings concerning the ordinations of Anglican Bishops; and secondly, the sentence brought on September 20th against Soanen , the Bishop of Senez . A certain pastoral Instruction had appeared under his name, teeming with infamous errors of every kind, and in which, as much as the work of Quesnel was commended, so much was the Bull condemning it prostituted as if worthy of every execration. Soanen, having initially prevaricated, once thirteen Bishops had been named before whom he might plead his cause—and against whom he himself had nothing to object—finally set out for Embrun, not without a profane retinue, and one that was not unarmed. But before he entered the city, he ordered it to be announced to the assembled group that he would never recognize them as judges. Subsequently, when asked by the Council whether that was indeed his Instruction, he did indeed deny that he had composed it, yet nonetheless openly professed that he entirely adopted, held, and approved it as his own, until he should be convinced of the errors which the Bishops had condemned in it. Indeed, the obstinacy of this man could not be overcome. For this reason, by the sentence of the Council, he was interdicted from every function, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese.  For my grandfather (which I see happens to many) to have been reduced to poverty, I bear it in my mind with my fortune somewhat aggrieved.  I, who have taken up the cause of my sorrow and assumed amendment for my sins, Lord Jesus Christ, with the multitude of those who sorrow and are truly penitent, and those who seek You in truth, I confess to You all my sins. Item, that no Confratre shall speak in the Chapter unless he has been questioned or called; if anyone does otherwise, he shall pay six Constance denarii as a penalty.

Noailles was still more terrified by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in defending its acts. In the year 1727, many bishops had gathered at Embrun to overthrow the immense errors that were being scattered everywhere by the schismatics, and to compose the disturbances incited by them. Furthermore, there were two principal acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer from the monastery of Saint Genevieve along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, who, intending to carry out the system of Dupin , crossed over into England and exalted himself there with other writings concerning the ordinations of Anglican bishops; the other act was the sentence passed on the 20th of September against Soanen, the Bishop of Senez . Under his name, a certain pastoral Instruction had appeared, teeming with shameful errors of every kind, and by which, as much as the work of Quesnel was commended, so much was the Bull condemning it held up as if it were worthy of every execration. The condemnation

Soanen, having initially prevaricated, and with thirteen Bishops having been named before whom he might plead his cause, and against whom he himself had no objections, finally set out for Embrun , not without a profane escort, and one that was not unarmed. But before he entered the city, he ordered it to be announced to those who had gathered that he would never recognize them as judges. Subsequently, when asked by the Council whether that Instruction was his, he indeed denied that it had been composed by him, yet nonetheless openly professed that he entirely adopted, held, and approved it as his own until he could be convinced of the errors which the Bishops had condemned within it. Therefore, by the sentence of the Council, he was interdicted from every function, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese. …nts and various pamphlets, two of which were accused of attacking episcopal authority or at least showing it too little deference. Sancyranus seized this opportunity to declaim against the regulars and issued that famous pamphlet on the *Hierarchy* under the pseudonym of *Petrus Aurelius*. The work was well-received as long as the author remained hidden, and it was approved by the Synod of the Gallican Clergy on April 27, 1641, and committed to the press at their expense. Antoine Godeau, Bishop of Grasse, added a eulogy in which the author is proclaimed an "invincible defender of bishops, a most fierce lover of the truth, a most just vindicator of the Hierarchy, and a theologian raised in the bosom of ancestral theology." Sancyranus's modesty did not have enough strength to allow him to remain hidden any longer amidst such commendation of himself and his work. But when the author was discovered, a blush covered their faces, and all that pomp of words eventually vanished even from the book *Gallia Christiana*.

Indeed, he proved himself a candidate of ancestral theology in the book condemned on April 23, 1654: *Familiar Theology, or a brief explanation of the mysteries of the Faith*

To pass over other fragments, the treatise of Augustini on Virginity, which he had edited with notes in the French idiom under the name of P. Seguenot, a priest of the Oratory, was fatal for him. On account of this, and also because he could no longer restrain himself, by the order of Cardinal Richelieu he was arrested together with Seguenot. In the same year and month in which Jansenius had died, on the 14th of May, he was committed to prison, from which, having been released after the death of the Cardinal, he did not stir any further. Shortly after, struck by an apoplexy on October 11, 1643, he departed to the majority .

But sinners do not possess charity: are they, therefore, not part of the Church?

Hæc iterum formula mox a Rege ad Parlamentum rursus mittitur tabulario inferenda, præcipitur omnibus Regni Præsulibus, & Ecclesiasticis ejusdem subscriptio, dictatur pœna jacturæ, seu confiscatio bonorum, amissionis beneficiorum, quin deportationis &c. Obtemperavit pars longe maxima Episcoporum, minasque pœnarum canonicarum addidit. Harduinus Perefixus eodem anno ad Archiepiscopatum Parisinum evectus inter primos mandatum subscriptionis per dioecesim suam vulgat, & anno sequente 1665. Portum Regium tam Parisinum, quam Campensem lustrat, Virgines ferocius renitentes una cum Agnete a S. Paulo Arnaldi forore, & Parthenonis Antistite ejicit, variisque monasteriis includit, cæteras, Sacramentis interdicit.

Quo doloris sensu factio nidum suum tam subito disturbatum viderit, facile est divinare. Trepidatio primum ingens, tum clamores: hinc tormenta, & lugubres threni persecutionem veritatis, & innocentiæ deplorantium; hinc diræ, quidquid sacræ profanæque dignitatis erat, devoventium: tumultuatum denique inter ipsas factionis partes, atque per plures annos præsentis sæculi usque decertatum. Sancyranus seized this opportunity to declaim against the regulars and issued that famous pamphlet on the *Hierarchy* under the pseudonym of *Petrus Aurelius*. The work was well-received as long as the author remained hidden, and it was approved by the Synod of the Gallican Clergy on April 27, 1641, and committed to the press at their expense. Antoine Godeau, Bishop of Grasse, added a eulogy in which the author is proclaimed an "invincible defender of bishops, a most fierce lover of the truth, a most just vindicator of the Hierarchy, and a theologian raised in the bosom of ancestral theology." Sancyranus's modesty did not have enough strength to allow him to remain hidden any longer amidst such commendation of himself and his work. But when the author was discovered, a blush covered their faces, and all that pomp of words eventually vanished even from the book *Gallia Christiana*.

Indeed, he proved himself a candidate of ancestral theology in the book condemned on April 23, 1654: *Familiar Theology, or a brief explanation of the mysteries of the Faith*

…, since the Son of God works everywhere, it must be that his flesh is present everywhere.* Answer. In this place, Osiander rehashes and casts back at us the first argument of the Apollinarian heretics, who attributed Deity to the flesh of Christ, just as a soul is attributed to a body. Furthermore, the very likeness used by Osiander overturns the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ. For just as a soul, even though hypostatically united to a body, does not exercise all its operations through the body, such as meditating, reasoning, and the like: so too the Deity of Christ does not perfect all its actions through his humanity, even after the union. Therefore, it does not conclude that it is present everywhere.

Harduinus Perefixus eodem anno ad Archiepiscopatum Parisinum evectus inter primos mandatum subscriptionis per dioecesim suam vulgat, & anno sequente 1665. Portum Regium tam Parisinum, quam Campensem lustrat, Virgines ferocius renitentes una cum Agnete a S. Quo doloris sensu factio nidum suum tam subito disturbatum viderit, facile est divinare. Trepidatio primum ingens, tum clamores: hinc tormenta, & lugubres threni persecutionem veritatis, & innocentiæ deplorantium; hinc diræ, quidquid sacræ profanæque dignitatis erat, devoventium: tumultuatum denique inter ipsas factionis partes, atque per plures annos præsentis sæculi usque decertatum. Hardouin de Péréfixe, elevated to the Archbishopric of Paris in the same year, was among the first to publish the mandate for subscription throughout his diocese, and in the following year, 1665, he inspected Port-Royal, both the Parisian and the Campanian houses. He cast out the nuns who resisted most fiercely, along with Agnes of Saint Paul, sister of Arnauld and Abbess of the convent, and confined them in various monasteries; he forbade the others from the Sacraments.

It is easy to divine with what sense of pain the faction saw its nest so suddenly disturbed. First there was a huge trepidation, then cries: on one side, torments and mournful laments of those deploring the persecution of truth and innocence; on the other, curses calling down divine wrath upon whatever sacred and profane dignity existed. Finally, there was turmoil among the very parts of the faction itself, and they struggled against one another for many years up to the present century. For since they were urged toward subscription everywhere by the vigilance of the Bishops as well as by the stern command of the King,

the rigid morality of many suffered no small blemish. They signed without shedding the error from their minds; they committed perjury so that they might be allowed to retain what was theirs or aspire to new things. Those who were of a more tender conscience, or wished to appear so, looked about for subterfuges and means by which they might mitigate the horror of perjury, and they resorted to equivocations and mental reservations, which even the most lax morality would abhor.

Sancyranus seized this opportunity to declaim against the regulars and issued that famous pamphlet on the *Hierarchy* under the pseudonym of *Petrus Aurelius*. The work was well-received as long as the author remained hidden, and it was approved by the Synod of the Gallican Clergy on April 27, 1641, and committed to the press at their expense. Antoine Godeau, Bishop of Grasse, added a eulogy in which the author is proclaimed an "invincible defender of bishops, a most fierce lover of the truth, a most just vindicator of the Hierarchy, and a theologian raised in the bosom of ancestral theology." Sancyranus's modesty did not have enough strength to allow him to remain hidden any longer amidst such commendation of himself and his work. But when the author was discovered, a blush covered their faces, and all that pomp of words eventually vanished even from the book *Gallia Christiana*.

Indeed, he proved himself a candidate of ancestral theology in the book condemned on April 23, 1654: *Familiar Theology, or a brief explanation of the mysteries of the Faith*

Here Osiander cooks up again and casts back at us the primary argument of the Apollinarian heretics, who attribute Deity to the flesh of Christ just as a soul is attributed to a body. Furthermore, this very comparison of Osiander overturns the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ. For just as the Soul, even when hypostatically united to the body, does not exercise all its operations through the body, such as meditating, reasoning, and the like: so too the Deity of Christ does not perfect all its actions through its humanity, even after the union. Therefore, it does not conclude that he is everywhere present.

THE OATH OF THE PRESIDENT.

I, N.N., as President and Commissioner deputed to this act of election, swear that I will act and conduct myself faithfully in this same act and that I will keep the secret. So help me God and these holy Gospels of God.

I, N.N., accepting the power granted to me by the Chapter at its request, swear that I will act and conduct myself faithfully in performing the scrutiny and that I will keep the secret. So help me God, and these holy Gospels of God.

I, N.N., canonically elected as Dean of this Chapter, pledge, vow, and swear to God Almighty, to the Most Blessed Virgin Mary, and to the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, the patrons of the same, that I will, to the best of my ability, defend and observe the rights, privileges, and customs of the aforementioned Chapter against all people, and that I will assist my confreres, both those present and those to come, with counsel and aid; nor will I receive any complaint from anyone against any of them, unless it be confirmed by two or three witnesses, according to the Apostle , who are beyond all exception. Excluding deceit and fraud. So help me God, and these holy Gospels of God.

…tiam alienos liberos baptizare possint. Quid ergo Sephorae exemplum ad Osiandri sententiam, cum contraria potius ex eo colligantur? Nimirum etsi vir adsit, posse mulierem baptizare non quofuis, sed suos tantùm liberos. Haec igitur est prima ad hoc exemplum Sephorae nostra responsio. Altera verò est, quod tum ex particulari generale quiddam colligit: tum ex facto extraordinario regula perpetua cōstituit, cùm nusquā alibi legamus mulieres in Dei populo, & sub lege suos vel alienos liberos circūcidisse. …that even if a husband is present, a woman is able to baptize, not just any children, but only her own. This, therefore, is our first response to this example of Zipporah. 

The second response is that he draws a general rule from a particular instance, and establishes a perpetual regulation from an extraordinary act, when we read nowhere else that women among the people of God, and under the Law, circumcised their own or others' children. Moreover, this was also done to the insult and rebuke of Moses himself. For the Lord, by that means, rebuked Moses through his wife for excessive negligence, because he had not circumcised his own sons, and had neglected that most sacred covenant of God with his family by omitting circumcision. Finally, who does not see that the nature of Baptism and Circumcision was different in this regard? We never read that the duty of Circumcision was once commanded by God specifically to the Priests, since Circumcision was instituted by God and practiced by the people more than four hundred years before the Priests were set apart from the rest of the people. Furthermore, Christ delegated the ministry of baptizing only to those to whom

All present and your office expect your duty. From this you can consider that even your enemies desire greatly to return into your favor.
